questions.prompt: A bare Node HTTP server receives application/json. What does it receive before application parsing?

choices.text: A readable body stream that application code or middleware must interpret.
A complete string in a single data event guaranteed by the JSON media type.
An already parsed JavaScript object because the Content-Type header is application/json.
A validated domain object with every required field guaranteed.

questions.explanation: Node handles protocol framing and streams body content. Application JSON parsing and validation are separate work.

sources.title: HTTP
sources.claim: Node HTTP exposes incoming bodies through readable streams and outgoing responses through writable operations; it parses message framing rather than JSON application payloads.

questions.prompt: A Node response writes several chunks and then ends. What must the application still reason about?

choices.text: HTTP headers can be changed at any time after the full body was written.
Response lifecycle and buffering rather than assuming each write is final delivery.
Every write maps to one complete application message for every client.
Every write has already reached the client application when it returns.

questions.explanation: Response writes participate in a stream. Headers, completion and backpressure have distinct lifecycle semantics.

sources.title: HTTP
sources.claim: Node HTTP exposes incoming bodies through readable streams and outgoing responses through writable operations; it parses message framing rather than JSON application payloads.

questions.prompt: The JSON parser accepts a body containing `{"quantity": "many"}`. What remains required?

choices.text: Validate the parsed shape and domain constraints before using quantity.
Call quantity.toString without checking whether that member is callable.
Trust quantity because the handler has a TypeScript interface for this body.
Trust quantity because syntactically valid JSON proves a valid integer.

questions.explanation: Parsing establishes JSON syntax, not business-valid data. req.body remains user-controlled.

sources.title: body-parser
sources.claim: Body parsers match configured media types, limit request sizes and populate req.body, but user-controlled properties and values remain untrusted and need validation.

questions.prompt: What does a parser size limit principally constrain?

choices.text: The numeric range allowed for every quantity value in the parsed body.
The allowed numeric value of every JSON quantity field.
The maximum size of the handler response after parsing.
The maximum accepted request body size.

questions.explanation: A body limit bounds parser input size. Field constraints and authorization are separate validation concerns.

sources.title: body-parser
sources.claim: Body parsers match configured media types, limit request sizes and populate req.body, but user-controlled properties and values remain untrusted and need validation.

questions.prompt: In Express 5, an async handler returned Promise rejects. What does the router do?

choices.text: It handles only explicitly caught rejections passed to next by application code.
It forwards the rejection to the error path as a next call.
It treats a rejection as an ordinary next() and skips error middleware.
It always waits for a separate manual next call before noticing rejection.

questions.explanation: Express 5 forwards errors from returned Promises. This does not cover unrelated asynchronous callbacks automatically.

sources.title: Error Handling
sources.claim: Express 5 automatically forwards rejected returned Promises to next; error middleware has four parameters, follows routes, and should delegate errors when headers have already been sent.

questions.prompt: A streamed response already sent headers when an error occurs. What should custom error middleware do?

choices.text: Replace the status and write a second JSON response as if nothing was sent.
Delegate with next(err) rather than attempting a second response.
Continue writing the old stream without observing any failure.
Mark the request successful because errors after headers never matter.

questions.explanation: Once headers are sent, custom handlers should delegate. A valid replacement response may no longer be possible.

sources.title: Error Handling
sources.claim: Express 5 automatically forwards rejected returned Promises to next; error middleware has four parameters, follows routes, and should delegate errors when headers have already been sent.

questions.prompt: Which bare Node HTTP body statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: HTTP message framing and application payload interpretation are distinct.
A JSON content type automatically validates every business field.
Application code must interpret JSON payload content.
Incoming request bodies can be consumed as a stream.
A data chunk is guaranteed to equal one complete JSON document.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: Node protocol parsing is not domain validation. B: Incorrect: headers do not validate payload semantics. C: Correct: explicit parsing is needed. D: Correct: IncomingMessage is readable. E: Incorrect: chunks can split or combine content arbitrarily.

sources.title: HTTP
sources.claim: The HTTP API streams message bodies and is deliberately low-level, not automatically interpreting application payload contents.

questions.prompt: Which boundary decisions make parsed requests safer to use? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Recognize that successful parsing does not establish domain validity.
Validate properties and types before invoking methods on them.
Configure a bounded input size for the parser.
Assume Content-Type proves the requester followed the required schema.
Treat every req.body property as trusted after parsing completes.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: syntax and domain constraints are separate. B: Correct: missing or malicious properties can fail. C: Correct: limits bound accepted payloads. D: Incorrect: media type is not schema enforcement. E: Incorrect: parsed values remain user-controlled.

sources.title: body-parser
sources.claim: req.body is untrusted; body parsers select configured content types and bound sizes but do not validate domain fields.

questions.prompt: Which Express 5 async-error claims are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A route rejection always results in automatic retry instead of error handling.
Errors in independent callback-based work still need to reach next explicitly.
A rejected Promise returned by a route enters the error-handling path.
A Promise rejection can be forwarded without a manual catch(next) wrapper.
Every later timer callback exception is automatically caught by its earlier route.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: forwarding is not retrying. B: Correct: callback errors must be passed into the error path. C: Correct: Express 5 forwards returned Promise failures. D: Correct: this is built-in for returned Promises. E: Incorrect: separate callbacks are outside that synchronous catch boundary.

sources.title: Error Handling
sources.claim: Express 5 automatically forwards rejected returned Promises to next; error middleware has four parameters, follows routes, and should delegate errors when headers have already been sent.

questions.prompt: Which custom error-middleware claims are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Define it as (err, req, res), since Express infers error handlers from parameter names.
Delegate an error when res.headersSent indicates a response has begun.
Place it after the routes and other middleware it handles.
Register it before every route to guarantee it receives downstream errors.
Its signature includes (err, req, res, next).

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: Express uses the four-argument error-middleware signature. B: Correct: another normal response cannot safely replace sent headers. C: Correct: downstream forwarding reaches the error handler. D: Incorrect: the documented order puts error handlers last. E: Correct: this distinguishes the error handler.
